<reason>Both sides argued competently, but CON built the cleaner and more decisive route. CON conceded the fairness premise (subsidies are regressive) and then attacked the specific operative element of the motion as written — the five-year clock — while offering a live alternative (reform the regressive tail immediately via tiered/lifeline pricing and industrial concessions, sequence full removal to audited delivery). That reframe is legitimate rather than evasive because the motion contains the deadline. CON's two sharpest instruments both landed: the "adequacy, coverage, savings — pick two" trilemma, which PRO partly conceded by saying "the gain need not be maximum immediate savings," and the paradox that every PRO safeguard (legal monthly indexation, displacement-based enrollment, pre-tranche top-ups) presupposes exactly the state capacity whose absence is the problem. Crucially, PRO's honest answer that subsidies should end at year five even if millions of displaced and undocumented households remain unenrolled gave CON its cleanest weighing line, and CON exploited it without distortion. PRO's best counters — that subsidies also fail to guarantee delivery to the poorest, that lifeline pricing still routes aid through fuel purchases rather than need, and that capacity-based thresholds invite indefinite postponement — are real and kept the debate competitive, but CON pre-empted the postponement worry with day-one tail reform and milestone-based conditionality, and PRO never squarely answered the presupposed-capacity paradox in its closing. CON also framed risk-bearing memorably (state absorbs the shock under subsidies, households absorb it under fixed transfers, including in Gulf states with sovereign funds). CON's two clipped turns are a real execution cost, and PRO's pressure questions were sharp, but they were answered directly with labels and substance. Net: a clear but competitive CON win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's use of PRO's own answer — "Yes, universal subsidies should end by year five" even with millions unenrolled — paired with the paradox that PRO's remedies for weak capacity (legal monthly indexation, displacement-based enrollment) all presuppose strong capacity. This crystallized the deadline as the harm-scheduling element and PRO never squarely dissolved it.</best_rebuttal>
